analysis.one_liner: Requires product makers to label packages when they shrink a product without cutting its price.
analysis.headline: The bill to require shrinkflation labels never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee from August 2024 until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill orders the Federal Trade Commission to write rules, within a year, requiring manufacturers to put a notice on packaging whenever they have shrunk a product without lowering the price by a matching amount. A violation would be treated as an unfair or deceptive practice under the FTC Act, so the agency could enforce it with its existing powers. The bill also authorizes $1 million to cover the cost of writing and enforcing the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers benefit: they would see a label when a package has quietly been downsized while the price stayed the same, making it easier to comparison-shop and hold brands accountable. The FTC would get a clear mandate and enforcement hook to police the practice.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a label on the package itself whenever a manufacturer has downsized a product without cutting the price by a commensurate amount, so consumers can see shrinkflation at the shelf instead of discovering it at home.
Makes violations enforceable as unfair or deceptive practices under the FTC Act, meaning the FTC can use its full enforcement toolkit, including penalties, against companies that skip the disclosure.
Gives the FTC flexibility to refine the definition of shrinkflation through its normal rulemaking process, and leaves the agency's other consumer-protection authority untouched.

analysis.who_pays: Packaged goods and consumer product manufacturers that use downsizing as a price increase would bear the cost of labeling (or the lost margin of shrinking less often), and taxpayers would fund the FTC's rulewriting through a $1 million authorization.

drawbacks.text: The bill only mandates disclosure; it does not ban shrinkflation or lower prices, so companies could keep downsizing as long as they tell shoppers they did.

The key term is left vague: manufacturers may argue about what counts as a price cut 'by a commensurate amount,' and the FTC would have to settle that through regulations, inviting disputes and slow implementation.

Compliance falls on manufacturers, who would have to track every size change and price across their product lines; small makers could face a heavier relative burden than large ones, and the bill authorizes only $1 million for the FTC's side of the work.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are modest but real: shelf-level transparency for a practice that is hard for shoppers to detect, at a stated public cost of just $1 million plus labeling compliance for manufacturers. The honest limitation is that disclosure is not a remedy — the bill leaves shrinkflation legal, so its value depends entirely on shoppers actually reading and reacting to the labels.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 2024 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never gave it a hearing or a vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, killing it automatically.

narrative.text: Rep. Ilhan Omar introduced the Shrinkflation Reduction Act on August 2, 2024, with 17 Democratic colleagues joining as original cosponsors, including Reps. Tlaib, Casar, Bowman, Bush, and Norton.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which is where the record ends — no subcommittee action, no markup, no floor vote is listed in its action history.
Because the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the committee acting, the bill died without ever being considered; bills do not carry over to a new Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Packaged goods and consumer product manufacturers that shrink products while holding prices are better off, because they face no federal labeling requirement. Shoppers are no better informed than before.

for.name: Rep. Ilhan Omar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and directed it to the FTC rulemaking approach.

for.name: 17 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or committee vote, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; the only partisan signal is that all 18 House supporters (the sponsor and 17 cosponsors) were Democrats and no Republican signed on.

industries.industry: Packaged food and consumer goods manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would force companies that quietly downsize products while holding prices to say so on the label, and make skipping the label an FTC-enforceable deceptive practice. Shrinkflation is a way of raising prices without an obvious price change, so disclosure directly threatens the strategy's value to the industry.
